• Name: Blue Moon crayfish (Cherax boesemani)
  • Other names: Cherax Blue Moon, Blue Papuan crayfish, Rainbow crayfish, Supernova crayfish, Blue Marble crayfish
  • Tank size (optimal): ~80 litres
  • Breeding: easy to medium
  • Diet: omnivore / carnivore as juveniles, omnivore / herbivore as adults
  • Temperament: aggressive
  • Life span: up to 5 years
  • Colour forms: beige, olivaceous brown, olivaceous green, reddish-brown, purplish, grey bluish, red to black with pinkish margins

Cherax boesemani is not very common in the aquarium trade, but it can be recommended even for beginners. It is hardy, easy to care for and can breed in captivity. It is generally available in Europe and rarely in the United States.

Make sure the species is not banned in your state and that you do not buy or sell it illegally. For example, the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (2017) does not allow it to be personally possessed, ported, purchased, sold, propagated, transported or used for commercial activities, because it is considered to have a high risk of becoming invasive. Even where it is not banned, NEVER release it into the wild.
Cherax boesemani is a crayfish endemic to West Papua, Indonesia. It is found only in the Ajamaru Lakes and the Ajamaru River, which belongs to the Kais River drainage.

These crayfish live in shallow areas (rarely more than 3 m deep) of the lakes with many plants, wetlands and tributaries. The lakes have hard, mineral-rich water with neutral pH.

The genus name Cherax is thought to be a misspelling of the Greek word 'charax', meaning a pointed stake, or a thing that scratches. The species was named after Dr. Marinus Boeseman, who contributed to the knowledge of Cherax crayfish in Irian Jaya (West New Guinea) and first collected it in 1955.

Because of its growth potential, Cherax boesemani needs a lot of space. A 20-gallon long tank (~80 litres) is recommended per adult crayfish.

All crayfish are very good escape artists: they climb vertical surfaces and are strong enough to move light lids, so a tight-fitting lid is essential.

Keeping Cherax boesemani is not complicated; the species is hardy and tolerates a range of water parameters. Make sure the tank is properly cycled and do a 15–20% water change a week.

To grow and restore lost limbs, the crayfish must molt regularly, and building a new exoskeleton requires a lot of calcium. Molting leaves them vulnerable, so provide many hiding places; in some cases a divider in the middle of the tank can protect them from tank mates. Do not remove molted exoskeletons.

Plants: Cherax boesemani is not plant safe. It will eat, cut, shred and uproot almost everything, so planted tanks are not recommended. Options are plastic plants, floating plants or cheap plants you are ready to lose.

Lifespan: there is no data for the wild; in captivity they can live 4–5 years if properly cared for.

• Temperature: 24–31°C, average 26°C. At lower temperatures metabolism slows down and they become even less active.
  • pH: 7.0–8.0 in the aquarium. In the wild, because of seasonal fluctuations, they have also been found in water with a pH of about 6.4.
  • Hardness: KH 3–20 and GH 3–25.

Substrate: no special requirements; any substrate will do.

Lighting: no special requirements; it is a nocturnal species.

Filtration: only hang-on-back and canister filters are suitable. Sponge filters are a bad idea, as the crayfish will chip, chew and break them apart.

Decorations and hiding spots: artificial shelters are essential and should be abundant. They offer protection during molting and the mating season, protect the broodstock against predation and minimise aggression. Examples: stacks of PVC pipes, coconut huts, mesh bundles, driftwood, stones. Crayfish do not like hiding spots with only one way out and prefer tight-fitting places.

Cherax boesemani is an opportunistic omnivore. In the wild it eats snails, insects, fish eggs, small fish, vegetables, aquatic plants, algae and detritus.

In captivity it needs a good mix of meat and vegetation, with about 15–20% protein in the diet. Adults are more herbivorous, whereas juveniles are more carnivorous; juveniles rely on protein for rapid growth and can become cannibalistic when protein is lacking.

Suggested foods:

  • leaves and plants
  • blanched vegetables (broccoli, cabbage, carrots, cucumber, lettuce, corn, spinach, peas, squash, leafy greens, etc.)
  • crushed snails
  • earthworms
  • tubifex worms
  • blackworms
  • bloodworms, including frozen
  • brine shrimp
  • dead fish or shrimp
  • shrimp food (shrimp pellets, granules, crustacean food such as Hikari Shrimp Cuisine)

Feeding frequency: 3–4 times a week.

  • Feed before lights out.
  • Leave food for 24 hours before removing it; siphon out leftovers before adding fresh food. Leaves can stay in the tank for several days.
  • Check hiding places from time to time, as they drag and store food there, which can cause bacterial contamination.
  • Vary the diet periodically.

Cherax boesemani has complex social behaviour. It is solitary and territorial, yet often found in close proximity to others. Its aggression is low compared with many other popular ornamental crayfish (blue crayfish, red crayfish, marbled crayfish, Cherax destructor, etc.), but when aggression occurs it happens rapidly. It displays its claws to indicate dominance before violent contact. Males are more aggressive and will likely attack tank mates.

Despite their size they are skittish and shy and do not like staying in the open. They are nocturnal: activity starts at dusk and gradually stops before sunrise. They are not natural diggers but can burrow in soft substrate, and they are very good escape artists.

Tank mates: it is risky to house several crayfish together; they are usually better kept alone. If kept in groups, use one male with 1–2 females, feed well and provide many hiding places; aggression still cannot be fully avoided.

Fish: no aggressive fish, no bottom-dwelling fish and no slow swimmers. Coexistence with fast top-dwelling fish is possible but not recommended.

Snails and shrimp: snails will become food. Adult crayfish usually ignore dwarf shrimp, which are too fast, but any molting shrimp is an easy meal.

Bad tank mates: any other crayfish, freshwater crabs and frogs.

The species is sexually dimorphic.

  • Claws: males have much larger and longer claws than females, and only males have a white patch on the yellow part of the claws.
  • Shape: females have a wide tail and a slightly bigger carapace.
  • Abdomen: males have two L-shaped appendages (claspers) behind the 5th (last) pair of walking legs. Females have a circular sperm receptacle between the bases of the last two pairs of walking legs.

• Maturity: depending on temperature, they mature at about 8–10 months old.
  • Mating: males initiate and use their claws to grasp and hold the female.
  • After fertilisation, eggs develop inside the mother's body for 4–6 weeks, then move outside onto the female's tail.
  • Eggs are fairly large: 3 mm long, 2 mm wide. The female cleans them and keeps them oxygenated with her appendages.
  • A female carries a little over 100 eggs on average; the number correlates with her size.
  • Depending on temperature, eggs hatch in 40–50 days.
  • Juveniles should be kept in a separate tank with the same water parameters. They need more protein than adults and can quickly turn cannibalistic without food.
  • Babies are secretive and hide most of the time. They start getting colour at around 2 months old.

Cherax boesemani can grow up to 12–15 cm, though some individuals are reported to reach 25 cm. Several colour morphs exist (orange, red, beige, greenish-gray), but blue or dark red to brown are the most common. Claws vary in colour: beige, olivaceous brown, olivaceous green, reddish-brown, purplish, grey bluish, red to black with pinkish margins and black tips; the uncalcified part is yellowish or pale to white. The claws are equal in form and size. Apart from its colour pattern and size, it is morphologically very similar to Cherax pulcher.

Its popularity seems to be rising. With striking coloration and hardy nature it makes a great aquarium pet if its diet and behaviour are understood. Check local laws, as it is banned in some places.
